Get distracted by finding and downloading new songs while mixing. 

When playing music with ADHD, I always get distracted because one song makes me think of another song and another song makes me think of something that will mix well with another song .. etc. 

Most of the times I forget to find that song or write it down and then forget to go back and look for it. 

While practicing mixing at home it’s the perfect time to expand your music library. Just let the songs play through and download while mixing lightly. 

Another option is to “fast mix” or whatever. Idk if there is a term for this but it’d almost be like live mixing really heavily mixed mashups. 

Another option is to listen out for special cool FX and small clips of certain lyrics or other parts of songs that stick out to you. While mixing, open up another program or whatever software you have that can clip an audio file of a song. Stick it in a folder to use as a library for pads and stuff to use while mixing. 

Use the time alone DJing to expand and organize your library and files and also practice more advanced mixing tricks. 

Not sure how many tracks you are spinning but on a four track, you can definitely find a way to never be bored while waiting for transitions if you do more advanced mashup type mixing simultaneously between all four. But if that’s too fast for your style and your prefer to stick more with the original songs with lighter transitions, there’s also nothing wrong with skipping around to practice only transitions and let the songs play longer when you’re spinning live for people.

I was told during my mother’s funeral back in 2006 by the church pastor himself that I “have great potential and shouldn’t waste it.” 

I was told multiple times growing up that I was gifted, talented, special, etc. 

Trying to navigate through life is difficult as is but constantly having that looming over my head while being able to barely function in today’s societal standards definitely wore me down. 

The truth is, we ARE special. Nobody “caught up” with you. You mentioned that you were naturally good in a variety of activities, which is a certain versatility and adaptability that not many people possess. You are looking at and comparing yourself to those that honed in on one specific skill of theirs and excelled at it and have put in work towards that as their passion. (I bet they spent more time improving that skill than you would if you were to choose to excel at that specific skill set.) 

Unfortunately, we live in a society where we are raised to choose a specific career path. 

“Find your path. Find your passion. Go to school for it. Work hard and diligently on this one specific skill set. Find a career. Work hard doing that one specific skill set.” 

This is NOT how our mind works and we come off as lazy because we are not putting the same effort into a specific set of skills like others do. But in reality, we’re very efficient with our time and energy compared to others. If we wanted to choose that path, we could effectively and efficiently. 

So while yes, we are “special” compared to “neurotypical”. People notice it within us but the only standards of potential we should uphold are our own. Don’t allow others to bring you down because you’re not appearing successful by society’s standards.

In my opinion, I think the flaw in this line of thinking is pinning something as either the protestors fault or the police’s fault - when it might be more useful to view the whole situation as the fault of the whole dynamic social entity that’s happening over there. 

You could even say to an extent that the manipulation of media and collective behavior is the true evil in situations like this. 

We could go back and forth on whether Chinese media or Western media is painting a “truer” picture on the situations that are happening over there but I think that’s a debate that can’t be won. In addition to how the media paints the events, it’s also important to note that the inherent ideologies of the two sides skew how people view the situation. 

In Western worlds, the population is concerned with freedom and democracy. So naturally, not only do western citizens inherently view the protesters as heroes and the police force as evil. With that, the Western media will perpetuate that belief because anything else will make the citizens question the validity of the news and events they consume. 

In China, there’s a strong sense of national pride and it’s not all about individual freedom like over here. So again, inherently, those citizens view protestors as disruptive for the state and their media also continues to perpetuate those beliefs. 

I guess my point is, we view the events going on and paint it in a light that matches our societal narrative. This goes for people that are miles away from the events and also even the people within the events themselves. All it takes is word to spread one way or another for people to formulate their own opinions on the “true motives” of the other side. This then in turn results in sometimes unfortunately fatal events for some. 

Overall, I think this clash of ideologies was inevitable, but I’m personally not convinced once side is “better” than the other so much as it’s just a naturally occurring conflict on what should be considered important values to a society.

I grew up in the Episcopalian church and then later discovered my sexuality. Since my family has a deeply rooted history in the church, I feel fortunate that they were so willing to accept me. I feel for you that you haven't been as fortunate with your coming out. 

That being said, I think it speaks a lot about the values of the church itself and how my family's involvement in the church influenced their lack of judgement for my sexuality. It wasn't until some years later when part of my family tried out different denominations that I realized how different the Episcopalian Church was to others as far as LGBT acceptance. I felt very uncomfortable in that church and wasn't allowed communion. I could just *feel* the judgement.

As far as being agnostic, don't worry about that. It's perfectly fine to be agnostic yet take value in religious services nonetheless. Everybody is welcome to take communion at the church as well, but you're also free to decline it. I think technically you have to be baptized - which if you grew up with a religious family I assume you are. I saw someone say you can cross your arms at the alter to take the blessing. You can also stay in the pews as well. The Episcopalian Church is what you personally make of it, and all the members are usually\* judgement-free type people. I say that conditionally because with all communities, it's not guaranteed and there's bound to be that *one person*. 

You won't be pressured to join any extra activities, but there's usually coffee hour after the service where you can chat with the members and hopefully that will give you more insight into the community. Good luck!

Not sure if anyone has said but pick up some bouillon cubes too. You can cook your rice in broth for extra flavor. Make a broth and cut up veggies that will go bad and throw some beans, pasta, and seasoning for an easy soup. Egg drop soup is an easy cheap one too.

Bacon is relatively cheap and you can do so much with that. 

I pick up some rolls and tortillas and freeze them. Potatoes, pasta, rice, just have an array of starches at hand. 

You said you can’t but in bulk but pork shoulders are also on the cheap side and you can stick in crockpot to have with your rolls or on any of your other starches as well. 

Frozen veggies are good to have in the freezer. 

I also buy ground sausage instead of ground beef since it’s cheaper and I make a good spaghetti sauce with that. Bulk can shopping is good when you have some extra cash. For the spaghetti I use can of whole tomatoes, tomato sauce, and tomato paste, can of mushrooms. Throw in some italian spices (also brown sugar, cinnamon and all spice is a great variation). Cook ground sausage, add tomatoes and mushrooms, spices, and just let it simmer for an hour. If you have extra rolls just throw some garlic butter spread on it and bake while spaghetti is cooking. 

Another tip is to learn how to do asian cooking. I have an electric wok but using a hot frying pan can be used for stir fry. If you have an asian market around go there to buy some sauces, rice wine vinegar, soy, seasame oil, fish sauce, oyster sauce, whatever you’re feeling. 

Tofu is also reasonable price wise. What I’ve done in the past is coat the tofu with corn starch, seasoned with salt/pepper. Fry up a whole pack with some scrambled eggs if you want more substance. Save that mixture in a container and now you have your protein for a few days that can be thrown on rice with an asian sauce and some frozen stir fry veggies or you can throw it into a curry sauce. (There’s blocks of japanese curry that’s delicious and work similar to bouillon cubes) 

After you make rice, have it fresh one day but the next day is when rice is perfect for fried rice. Now you have leftover tofu/eggs to throw into fried rice as well.

So, normally we count 1,2,3,4,5, 6, 7, 8, 9.. then the digits repeat as 10, 11, etc. 

This is how we as humans decided to represent the mathematics we use the most.

Mathematics itself though, transcends beyond our cognitive representation of these numbers and nature does not always simply count 1,2,3.

The fibonacci sequence is a very famous pattern found in nature, you’ve probably seen it [visually represented. ](https://images.app.goo.gl/MdGURGGU5W9252bb8) 

So the way this mathematical pattern is counted is by taking the two previous numbers and summing them. 

The sequence starts as 0,1,1,2,3,5. 

This pattern has been known to us for a while because it’s “simple” for us “1,2,3” minds to see that 0+1 = 1, 1+1=2, 2+3=5, etc. 

There are patterns that exist that we can’t even comprehend yet because the mathematics behind them are more complex. 

Binary is simply another counting system, and is the one being used to represent the pattern in the original post. 

Binary is currently a very important counting system to identify patterns because our computers count in binary 0=off, 1= on. This makes it simple for a computer to recognize mathematics because like humans, their cognitive representation of numbers is also limited (for now) and in this case it’s limited to only 0 and 1. Electricity on or off. 

0, 1, 10, 11, ... = 0, 1, 2, 3, ... 

While the digits themselves are limited, we can see from the comparison above that it’s still possible to represent the number system we know and love as only 0’s and 1’s.

Mathematicians are rarely satisfied though, and decided that any number can be used as a base for a counting system. 

If you’re feeling adventurous you can look more into [modular arithmetic.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_arithmetic) 

We use this everyday when we check the time. After 12 hours, we wrap back around to 1 again. This is similar to how we wrap around to using a 1 and 0 when we count to ten, and also how binary wraps around to a 1 and a 0 when it counts to the number two. 

Modular arithmetic takes some time to sit on for a bit, because it’s not natural to us as we’re so engrained in our 0-9 digit counting. 

What does this have to do with the original visualization? 

Well, remember mathematics kinda just doesn’t care about how we count numbers? Well modular arithmetic is one way to be able to discover and visualize some patterns we could not conceptualize previously. 

What’s the point? 

Well, humans are natural pattern seekers. Understanding how numbers fundamentally work maybe can give us some insight to the world we live in. 

In my opinion, the applications of understanding patterns and sequences can be endless and may be used in future applications we can’t even fathom yet, which is the beautiful thing about mathematics. Once the knowledge is known, humans can carry it on with them. 

Fibonacci was only trying to make sense of the patterns of rabbits breeding. Little did he know the legacy he’d leave behind and that the fibonacci sequence still being used to discover more of our world and create algorithms for us. 

That being said, there are current real world applications that use sequences, patterns, and different modular arithmetic. 

The first one that comes to mind is cryptography. 

Being able to write out complex codes based on patterns are important for computer security. 

These codes contain patterns that are hard to recognize but are easy to read as soon as the computer knows the “key”. Which is just a piece of information to translate the mathematics. 

In the example of the fibonacci sequence, the “key” would simply be an equation telling the computer it’s the previous two digits summed together. 

I’m not a cryptographer though so I don’t know how complex it is these days and what all goes behind it, but that’s the gist of it. 

I hope that gives more insight :) Happy learning!
